title: Case study: the Namib coast (Swakopmund and Walvis Bay)

blocks.heading: What this section covers
blocks.text: One required case study of an area of coastline: the opportunities it presents, its hazards, and how far the hazards are managed - the Namib coast around Swakopmund and Walvis Bay.

blocks.heading: Opportunities: Swakopmund and Walvis Bay
blocks.text: Walvis Bay, about 30 kilometres south of Swakopmund on Namibia's Atlantic coast, owns the country's main deep-water port; its new container terminal opened in 2019, and the town is the heart of Namibia's fishing and fish-processing industry, with salt works on the pans to the south. Swakopmund, founded as a colonial port in 1892, lives mainly on tourism: its sea-front hotels, shore angling, dolphin cruises out of Walvis Bay, and trips into the dune belt behind the town.

blocks.heading: The hazards of the Namib coast
blocks.text: The coast is desert - rainfall is usually below about 20 millimetres a year - yet the hazards still arrive. The cold Benguela Current offshore cools the moist air into fog on many days each year, and the fog is a hazard to travel on the coast road. The dune belt between the two towns is mobile: the prevailing south-west wind blows the dry sand inland, over fencing and onto the road that crosses it. And at Swakopmund the low sea front is eroded by high tides and storms.

blocks.heading: Managing the hazards
blocks.text: Management protects where people and trade gather. Swakopmund's sea front is defended by a stone promenade that works as a sea wall, and the town's buildings behind it have stood for more than a century. The road across the dune belt has to be kept clear of drifting sand, and the port's breakwaters shelter Walvis Bay's harbour. Beyond the built-up ground the dunes are left to move as they will, because defending empty desert is not worth the cost - a judgement that shows management is a decision about where to spend, not a wall along the whole coast.

blocks.heading: Where this connects
blocks.text: This case study answers the Paper 1 case-study question on coasts: learn the two towns, the container terminal of 2019, the dune belt, the Benguela fog and the sea-front promenade as the place-specific detail. Pair it with the processes of the first section - the sea front is a cliff-and-defence story, and the dunes are the wind's deposition, taught earlier in this topic - and the management theme runs on through Rivers, topic 2.2, and into Theme 3.
